claim: Changing the default moves stated organ-donation consent by about 40 points in the one-shot online experiment (opt-in 42%, opt-out 82%, forced choice 79%, N=161) and country registries show the same split (explicit consent 4-27%, presumed consent 86-99.98%). Cross-checker re-opened the paper: numbers confirmed.
schema_part: S0 gate / S7 selection: a default is a hidden anchor
agent_test: Run the same item with the default option placed first, second, or absent (forced choice); measure how often the answer follows the default.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: In the donation experiment opt-out was not different from forced choice; the harm sits in the opt-in default, so a no-default control is needed to see the direction of a default effect.
agent_test: Add a no-default arm to every anchor or default test on the agent.

claim: Nudge meta-analysis headline: pooled d about 0.43-0.45 over 200+ papers and 2.1 million people; decision-structure nudges (defaults etc.) are larger than information or assistance nudges, with food largest and finance smallest.
schema_part: none (context: structural changes beat informational ones)
agent_test: Not agent-testable; use as a prior that structural changes beat informational ones.

claim: After publication-bias adjustment the pooled nudge effect shrinks sharply: severe-bias d about 0.08, moderate 0.31 (Mertens reply, Szaszi), RoBMA 0.04-0.11 with the interval touching zero (Maier). Whether nudges work on average is contested, and heterogeneity is huge (prediction interval about -0.48 to 1.39).
schema_part: none; warns against trusting single published human debiasing effects
agent_test: When importing a human debiasing effect into the scaffold, test it on our agent before keeping it; assume the published size is inflated.

claim: At scale, nudge units' 126 RCTs (23 million people) give 1.4 percentage points (about 8% over control), versus 8.7 points in published academic nudge papers; selective publication and low power explain most of the gap (corrected academic estimate 3.2 points). Nudge-unit trials excluded default changes.
agent_test: Prior for effect size: expect much less than the papers claim.

claim: Reference class forecasting (outside view): infrastructure projects have large, persistent optimism error (mean cost overrun rail 44.7%, bridges/tunnels 33.8%, roads 20.4%; rail passenger forecast 51.4% too high on average, 84% of rail forecasts off by more than 20%; no improvement over decades). Numbers re-opened and confirmed.
schema_part: S0 gate / S7 selection: base rate from class record
agent_test: Give the agent a plan-estimate task with and without a class record of past similar tasks; compare estimate error.

claim: Method of the outside view: pick the class, get the outcome distribution, place the project in it, then apply an uplift chosen by the acceptable risk (UK DfT: roads 15% at 50% and 32% at 80% certainty; rail 40% and 57%; 68% for rail at 10% risk).
agent_test: Have the agent output a percentile of the class distribution instead of a point guess; score calibration.

claim: Prompting people to first think of the class (outside-view prompt) cut but did not remove overconfidence: students expected to beat 84% of peers; a prior prompt lowered ratings about 20%, still too high.
agent_test: Ask the agent for confidence after a base-rate question vs without; compare Brier scores.

claim: Flyvbjerg 2013 benchmark: the outside-view forecast cuts the spread of demand forecast error from 33% to 9.1% and the chance of a 15%+ shortfall from 80% to 5%. This is a conditional benchmark, not a controlled trial.
agent_test: Replicate with simulated reference classes of known outcomes.

claim: Accountability and financial-incentive reviews (Lerner and Tetlock 1999; Camerer and Hogarth 1999) were never opened by any agent; effects are known only from memory and cannot be used as evidence. Gap search: a 266-experiment systematic review (Aleksovska 2019) says accountability mostly raises effort and weakens biases (vote counts, no effect sizes), works better if announced before the task, lowers overconfidence, and worsens the dilution effect. Lerner and Tetlock full text still unopened.
agent_test: Read both reviews; then test an accuracy-demanding frame versus a justification frame on the agent.

claim: Planning fallacy numbers (Buehler, Griffin, Ross 1994) and 401(k) default numbers (Madrian and Shea 2001) are recalled from memory only and cannot be used as evidence yet. Gap search opened Madrian and Shea (NBER w7682): participation 37% (opt-in) vs 86% (auto-enrol) at 3-15 months; 76% of auto-enrolled stuck at the 3% default rate; 61% at the full default; non-default share rose 7% to 37% in 15 months. Buehler numbers (33.9 predicted vs 55.5 actual days, 30% on time) seen only in a secondary source.
agent_test: Open both papers before citing.

claim: Defaults meta-analysis (Jachimowicz et al. 2019): 58 studies, n=73,675, d=0.68 [0.53, 0.83], with two negative studies, larger for endorsement and status-quo readings and in consumer domains. Abstract-level only, not publication-bias corrected; Maier's corrected structure estimate (0.12 [0.00, 0.43]) suggests it is inflated.
agent_test: Open the paper.

claim: LLMs show human-like anchoring: low and high anchors move estimates (ChatGPT high anchor 105.97 vs low 20.83); Codex estimates equal the anchor exactly 67% of the time; irrelevant context cuts Codex accuracy by 22-31 points. One study (Lou and Sun) found GPT-4 anchoring index 0.45 vs 0.61 in a human-style study, and time questions not significant.
agent_test: Run a numeric estimation battery with random anchors; count shift toward anchor, with and without our guardrail.

claim: Telling an LLM to ignore the anchor or simply warning it (awareness) gives mixed results: awareness cut GPT-4 anchoring distance 0.250 to 0.105, but the same prompts left GPT-4 framing bias unchanged or worse (-0.405 to -0.470), and a bandwagon mitigation raised GPT-3.5 bias from 0.524 to 0.955; order bias was not fixed by any method.
schema_part: G guardrails (do not rely on a generic warning)
agent_test: Compare a warning line vs a structural change (re-ask with the anchor removed) on the same items at equal tokens.

claim: Structural debiasing of LLM inputs and procedure (self-help re-asking, abstention plus bias inspection) works better than a plain warning for strong models: GPT-4 residual biased prompts 0% to 2.7%; abstention plus specific-bias inspection reached 93.5% accuracy on the 205-item BRU set; weaker models (GPT-3.5) stay at 8-17% biased.
agent_test: Add a self-help re-ask step (rewrite prompt without bias cues) and measure vs plain prompt at equal tokens.

claim: Few-shot examples and contrastive/counterfactual prompting made some LLM biases worse (GPT-4 anchoring distance 0.300-0.383 vs baseline 0.250); mitigation is model- and bias-specific.
schema_part: none (negative result: do not add generic mitigations)
agent_test: Log per-bias effect of each added scaffold step; drop steps that worsen any bias.

claim: Base-rate neglect is severe in LLMs: with a standard prompt GPT-4 was correct on only 15% of 40 base-rate items, LLaMA3-70B 10%; sunk cost 0%, overconfidence 10%.
agent_test: Base-rate items with and without a supplied class record; measure the gain.

claim: Chain of thought removes much cognitive-reflection error (GPT-3 5% correct, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, GPT-4 96% on 150 CRT tasks), but it does not fix anchoring (Lou: ignore-anchor failed).
agent_test: Run CRT and anchor items with and without CoT at equal tokens.

claim: LLM forecasting with retrieval and ensembling nears the human crowd but does not beat it: Brier .179 vs crowd .149 (random .250, best plain GPT-4 .208). Cross-checker re-opened the paper: confirmed. Retrieval and fine-tuning give most of the gain (without both .206); the reasoning prompt alone gave a minor gain.
schema_part: S0 gate / S7 selection (outside view with retrieval)
agent_test: Retrieval-of-class-record ablation on forecasting questions; Brier at equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: System beats the crowd when the crowd is unsure (crowd .3-.7: .199 vs .246) and is worse near 0/1 and on some platforms; averaging system and crowd is better than either.
schema_part: S7 selection (combine machine with outside estimate)
agent_test: Blend agent estimate with a base-rate estimate by weight; compare.

claim: A crowd of 12 LLMs matches a human crowd on 31 binary questions (Brier 0.20 vs 0.19, p=.85, preregistered; re-opened and confirmed); showing GPT-4 or Claude 2 the human median improved Brier (.17 to .14; .22 to .15). LLM mean forecast was biased above 50%.
schema_part: S7 selection (aggregation, anchor to outside view)
agent_test: Give the agent the class base rate as an anchor; check Brier change and acquiescence above 50%.

claim: ForecastBench: on 200 questions superforecasters (Brier 0.096) and the public (0.121) vs Claude 3.5 Sonnet (0.122); best LLM without crowd forecast on market questions 0.136.
agent_test: Use as a ceiling check for forecasting tests.

claim: Incentive-like prompts (emotion stimuli, tips, politeness, penalties) have uneven effects: EmotionPrompt relative gain 9.58 (Vicuna) down to 0.85 (GPT-4); tipping helped Llama-7B and not ChatGPT; a $1000 tip lowered accuracy. Incentives for LLMs are prompt text, not payoffs.
schema_part: none (do not add incentive text; section 4b)
agent_test: Compare a neutral prompt with an incentive line at equal tokens on a held-out set; expect small or no gain for strong models.

claim: Accountability (Lerner and Tetlock) has not been tested on LLMs in any retrieved study, and no study has an LLM agent fetch a reference class and compute its outcome rate. This is a search gap, not proof of absence. Gap search still found no LLM study of an accountability or stakes line measuring calibration. Human analogues: accountability lowers overconfidence (review), and a $0.50 vs $0.01 bonus lowered overreliance on a wrong AI (N=114).
agent_test: Build the first test: agent with and without a retrieved class record, scored by Brier.

claim: Default effects shrink with decision time: in one preregistered nationally representative experiment (N=637) the action-default gain was 86% vs 66% at short times and 66% vs 64% at long times; a mini meta-analysis (N=2,359) gives an interaction d=1.19 [1.06, 1.32].
schema_part: S7 selection: deliberation budget reduces default and anchor pull
agent_test: Run the default/anchor items with a short vs long reasoning budget and compare how often the answer follows the default.

claim: Forcing a human to commit before seeing AI advice reduces following wrong advice (chi2(2)=44.35, N=663 incorrect-AI trials, carb task) but does not raise team accuracy overall and is the least liked design; overreliance is a cost-benefit choice that falls when checking is cheap on a hard task and when the bonus is higher.
schema_part: S7: commit-first then compare with the class record
agent_test: Compare (a) show class record first, (b) commit estimate then show class record, (c) no record; measure error vs truth and anchoring on the record.

claim: Mitigations are model-dependent in LLMs: self-help rewriting beat awareness, few-shot and counterfactual prompts for prompt-induced bias in 2023 models (works on GPT-4, weak on GPT-3.5 and Llama); awareness helped some evaluator biases but order bias did not clearly change; asking the model to answer as most people would made the bandwagon effect much worse.
schema_part: S0 gate: choose structural rewrite over warning line; avoid majority-opinion steps
agent_test: Rerun self-help rewrite, awareness line and no mitigation on the current model for anchoring, framing and order items.

claim: A 20-model benchmark (30,000 tests) finds average anchoring 0.39 and framing 0.41, status-quo bias strongly negative (-0.42), and a planning-fallacy updating test near zero or negative (GPT-4o -0.16): LLMs given the class overrun rate mostly use it, so the weak step is class selection and retrieval, not applying the base rate.
schema_part: S0 gate / S7: outside view is applied if the class record is supplied
agent_test: Give the agent a correct vs a wrong-but-plausible reference class and measure forecast error for each; the gap shows the cost of class choice.

claim: No study was found that tests an agent-retrieved reference class against a base-rate prompt at equal tokens, nor a non-infrastructure failed replication of reference class forecasting; Lovallo et al. 2012 is the candidate source and was not opened.
agent_test: Run the equal-token ablation described in K28 on our own task record.
